metaDescription: Helping travellers manage money abroad with a faster, clearer, and more trustworthy mobile experience.

hero.title: TUI Travel Money App, Redesigning a travel finance tool for modern travellers
hero.summary: TUI's travel money app hadn't been updated in years and no longer matched what users expect from a financial tool. This project redesigns onboarding, navigation, and core money flows to make the app feel as modern and reliable as leading fintech apps, while keeping the light holiday-ready tone TUI customers expect.

blocks.html: TUI offers currency exchange and prepaid travel cards to UK customers, but the app's outdated design and unclear flows were eroding user confidence. I led the redesign of onboarding, navigation, and the core money flows — card ordering, top-ups, and currency conversion — while also running competitive analysis and usability testing to validate direction.

blocks.title: My responsibilities
items: Led the redesign of onboarding and app navigation.
Simplified card ordering, top up, and currency exchange journeys.
Conducted competitive analysis, usability testing, and prototype validation.
Collaborated with engineering through implementation and QA.

blocks.title: Early signals being tracked
items: Task success rate for onboarding, top-ups, and currency conversion

items.challenge: Outdated interface and difficult navigation reduced confidence

items.goal: Monitor spending and exchange money efficiently
items.challenge: Exchange and fee information wasn't transparent or easy to find

blocks.html: The core tension: TUI needed an app that felt as trustworthy and capable as a modern banking tool, but most users first encounter it at the moment of booking a holiday — a mindset built around excitement, not financial admin. The experience had to earn trust fast without slowing people down.
Research combined stakeholder workshops, competitive benchmarking, and usability testing of the live product to identify the highest-friction journeys.

items.finding: Lengthy onboarding reduced confidence before users reached core features.
items.insight: Simplified onboarding into shorter, guided steps with clearer copy and reduced verification friction.

items.finding: Hidden navigation and fragmented account information made money management difficult.
items.insight: Rebuilt navigation around balances, cards, and transfers, with aggregated balances and dedicated currency wallets.

items.finding: Top-up and conversion forms buried key info in unclear, repetitive fields.
items.insight: Streamlined into guided flows with upfront FX rates and stronger visual hierarchy to reduce cognitive load and input errors.

blocks.html: The hardest tradeoff was balancing banking-grade clarity against a travel-friendly, lightweight feel — leaning too far toward either risked feeling either untrustworthy or overly clinical.
I structured the redesign around a single strategic principle: earn trust before asking for it. Every screen needed to either deliver value or build confidence — ideally both.

I mapped the existing 11-step flow and identified which steps could be deferred until after activation, parallelized, or eliminated entirely. The new flow reduced mandatory pre-activation steps from 11 to 4.
I ran two rounds of design sprints with the PM and engineering lead, each producing 3–4 high-fidelity prototypes for unmoderated Maze tests. Below are representative screens from Rounds 1 and 2.

The final design restructured onboarding into three phases: Explore, Commit, and Optimize. Users reach the dashboard after just two screens. Everything else happens contextually, when the user has a reason to care.

items.html: Demo mode first — New users land in a read-only demo dashboard populated with sample data. They see the product before giving anything.
Progressive permission requests — Bank connection is requested only when a user tries to add a real account, with explicit "why we need this" copy and security badges.
Step indicator — A minimal progress bar with labeled steps eliminates uncertainty. Tested three variants; the labeled version outperformed the bare progress bar by 18%.
Inline validation — Form fields validate as the user types, catching errors before submission and reducing frustration-induced abandonment.

blocks.html: The redesigned flow shipped to 100% of users in Week 14. Results were measured over the following 8 weeks.

items.label: Increase in bank account connection rate
D7 retention improvement for cohorts post-launch

blocks.html: The demo mode was an unexpected hit — 38% of users who entered demo mode went on to create a full account within the same session, a conversion rate the team hadn't seen for any previous acquisition channel.

The biggest shift in my thinking from this project: the best onboarding doesn't feel like onboarding. When users are exploring a product rather than completing a form, their defenses drop. Trust follows experience, not explanation.

I also learned to fight harder for research time early in the process. The usability sessions in Week 1 surfaced the "trust gap" framing that ultimately drove every major design decision. Without that, we'd have been optimizing copy rather than rethinking the architecture.
"The best onboarding doesn't feel like onboarding — it feels like using the product."
